I saved all eight answers to `answer.json`. The monthly totals, Q3 order count (1,315) and customer count (249) match between a Python run and a separate SQL query. One judgment call could change answer a, so check it before you rely on that one.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| a. Q3 segment with the highest net sales | `smb`, 323,213,832 |
| b. Customers with a paid order in Q3 | 249 |
| c. Q3 category with the highest net sales | `acc`, 330,399,373 |
| d. Month with the highest net sales, all periods | 2025-07 (321,007,195) |
| e. Customer with the largest Q3 refund total | u230@ex.com (2,271,000) |
| f. Customers with 2+ paid orders in Q3 | 233 |
| g. Average net sales per Q3 paid order | 706,264 |
| h. Growth from August to September | −5.9% (313,179,340 → 294,550,721) |

**Decision for you on a:** 32 of the emails shared by more than one account have different segments on those accounts. Your rules don't say which segment such a person belongs to. I gave each order's sales to the segment of the account that placed it, which makes `smb` the top segment. If you instead give each person the segment of their earliest account (lowest ID), `consumer` comes out on top with 340,816,305. If that rule fits your intent better, tell me and I'll update a.

The other data checks found nothing that changes the results:
- **Status values:** only `paid`, `pending` and `cancelled` appear.
- **Refunds:** every refund matches an order line, never exceeds the quantity ordered, and appears only once per line.
- **Times:** all timestamps are stored in the same UTC format, and I converted them to Korean time (UTC+9).

STATUS: DONE
